questions.q: What is the core idea behind "special-case reduction" for verifying a new implementation like a custom loss function?
options: Running the implementation on the full dataset and checking the final accuracy
Finding a narrower case of the general implementation where the correct output is analytically known, even if the general case isn't
Asking a colleague to manually review every line of code
Comparing the output to a random baseline
questions.explain: Special-case reduction finds a case with a known analytical answer (e.g., a KL-divergence loss comparing a distribution to itself should be exactly zero) to test the implementation, even when the general case has no known ground truth.

options: That the model's predictions match a labeled ground-truth dataset
That a custom backward pass's analytical gradient numerically agrees with a finite-difference estimate of the gradient, independent of whether the output is meaningful
That the model will generalize well to new data
That the loss function is convex
questions.explain: gradcheck checks internal consistency between a custom forward and backward implementation by comparing the analytical gradient to a numerical finite-difference estimate — it says nothing about whether the output values themselves are meaningful.

questions.q: In the permutation-invariance test example, what does the assertion actually check?
options: That the model's output matches a known correct value
That the model produces the same output when the order of elements in the input set is shuffled, which is a known relationship rather than a known value
That the model's loss decreases over training
That the gradients are non-zero
questions.explain: Invariance tests don't require knowing the correct output for any single input — they check a known relationship between two outputs (same output for a permuted input), which is enough to catch a bug if it fails.

questions.q: What does successfully overfitting a tiny batch to near-zero loss actually demonstrate?
options: That the model will generalize well to unseen data
That gradients are flowing correctly and the training pipeline isn't silently broken — but nothing about generalization
That the learning rate is optimally tuned for the full dataset
That the model has no numerical issues under mixed precision
questions.explain: Overfitting a tiny batch only verifies that the pipeline is wired correctly and gradients reach the right parameters. It says nothing about whether the model generalizes to data outside that tiny batch.

questions.q: Why is comparing a fast, vectorized implementation against a slow, naive reference implementation on small identical inputs a useful correctness check?
options: Because the fast implementation is always correct and the comparison is only useful for benchmarking speed

Because the naive implementation is easy to trust as correct (since it directly follows the mathematical definition), so agreement between the two on small inputs is strong evidence the fast version is also correct
Because it eliminates the need for any other correctness checks
Because it only works when ground-truth labels are available
questions.explain: A naive, loop-based implementation that directly follows the mathematical definition is slow but easy to trust. Agreement with a faster, more complex implementation on small test inputs provides strong evidence the fast version is correct, without needing labeled ground truth.
